questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: separate three words that share one English gloss by their register and topic
questions.stem: A learner is choosing between three Chinese words that all translate as to talk, and wants to know which one a speaker would use for a friendly chat with a friend over tea rather than for a work report. Which word is the chat one?

options.text: The word for chatting, since a friendly exchange has no agenda to discuss
The word for discussing, since any exchange of views counts as a discussion
options.misconception: treats a casual conversation as though it were a formal discussion

options.text: The word for speaking, since the general verb is always preferred in speech
options.misconception: assumes the general verb is the natural choice in informal conversation

options.text: All three are interchangeable, and the choice between them is only regional
options.misconception: believes register differences in a word set are only matters of place

questions.explanation: The three words divide the work by what the talk is for. The general verb covers simply speaking, and it is what you use when nothing more needs saying. The word for discussing carries a subject matter and a slightly official air, so it turns up in meetings, in the phrase for talking about work, and in reports. The word used in the compound for chatting is reserved for talk whose point is the company rather than the content, which is why it takes a social object instead of a topic. The temptation is to treat all three as synonyms because English uses one short word for the whole range.
questions.hint: Ask whether the talk has a subject matter, or whether the company is the point.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: sort four time words by the stretch of time each one names
questions.stem: A writer needs two different words, one for a stretch of decades within a century and one for time as a general measurable thing. Which pair does the language actually use?

options.text: The word for decades, and the word for time in general as a measurable thing
The word for time in general, and the word for decades of a century
options.misconception: swaps the two while keeping the idea that they name different stretches

options.text: The word for an occasion, and the word for an era of history as a whole
options.misconception: picks an occasion word and an era word instead of the right pair

options.text: The word for an era, and the word for an occasion or a point in time
options.misconception: chooses the two coarsest time words rather than the two wanted

questions.explanation: Four related words are in play and each has its own scale. The word for an occasion names a point or a stretch inside a day, as in at that time. The word for time names the general thing you can spend or lose. The word for decades names a numbered stretch inside a century, so the nineteen-eighties and the nineteen-nineties each take it. The word for an era names a large historical stretch, such as an age of thought or an age of expansion, and it usually carries a judgement. A learner who reaches for the era word when the meaning is a numbered decade has overshot by a whole register.
questions.hint: Ask how wide the stretch of time is, and whether a century can be divided by it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: separate a word for a national economy from one for being thrifty
questions.stem: A dictionary gives two English words, economy and economical, and a learner has to find the Chinese word for each one. Which pairing of English and Chinese is right?

options.text: Economy with the word for a country's finances, and economical with thrifty
Economy with the word for being thrifty, and economical with a country's finances
options.misconception: assigns the thrifty sense to the word that names a national economy

options.text: Both English words with the same Chinese one, since the language has a single term
options.misconception: assumes the language has one word where English separates two ideas

options.text: Both with a third word about saving, and with nothing naming a country's finances
options.misconception: misses the national sense entirely and answers with saving money

questions.explanation: The word that looks like a cognate of economy names a country's finances and belongs to the vocabulary of development and policy. The idea of being thrifty with money is a different word, and a related pair of words about cutting back and about saving up go with it. A learner who assumes a shared shape means a shared meaning reads the second English word straight onto the first Chinese word and produces a sentence about national finances when the intended sentence was about a household budget. The words do look alike in the two languages, which is exactly what makes them a trap rather than an easy pair.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two English words could be followed by the word growth.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: reject a romantic reading of a word used in a wedding notice
questions.stem: A learner reads a wedding notice that uses a two-character word for the couple and concludes that the notice announces a partner outside marriage. What does the word actually mean there?

options.text: The spouse or a loved one, and it does not mark a relationship as unmarried
A lover in the sense of a partner who is not yet married to them
options.misconception: takes the word as English uses the English cognate of it

options.text: A person who loves somebody, used here exactly as a verb would be used
options.misconception: reads a noun in a noun slot as though a verb had been placed there

options.text: An admirer, meaning somebody who admires a famous person from afar
options.misconception: reaches for the sense about distant admiration instead of a marriage

questions.explanation: In a wedding notice the two characters mean the husband and wife, in either order, and they are also used more widely for somebody a person loves, including a child or a friend. What the word does not do is single out a relationship that is not yet a marriage, which is the sense an English reader gets from the cognate and which is why a learner reads the notice wrongly. The same false-friend logic applies to the general word for friend, which covers any friend at all and so needs a separate word when a romantic partner is meant.
questions.hint: Ask what the two characters would be doing in a document about a marriage ceremony.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: reject a narrow English reading of the general word for friend
questions.stem: A learner translates the general Chinese word for friend as boyfriend and uses it in a message about a woman's romantic partner. What exactly has the learner got wrong?

options.text: The word means a friend in general, so it does not mark a romantic relationship
The word is correct, and it covers a romantic partner as well as a friend
options.misconception: assumes one word carries both the general and the romantic sense

options.text: The word is used only for women, and a man would need a different one
options.misconception: believes the word for friend is restricted to one gender

options.text: The word marks a friend of the same sex, so it excludes romantic partners
options.misconception: reads the general word as though it carried a same-sex restriction

questions.explanation: The word covers a friend of any kind, at any age, of either sex, and the relationship it names is friendship, so translating it with the narrower English word adds a meaning the original does not have. When a romantic partner is meant, the language uses a different word built on a word for younger woman or younger man, and adding the word for like before the general word is another way of softening the description. The general word is extremely frequent, and a learner who replaces it with the narrow one loses the ordinary sense in the far more common case of an actual friend.
questions.hint: Ask how many kinds of relationship the single word has to cover in a normal conversation.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: sort words for the cost of something by meaning and by register
questions.stem: Three descriptions of one market stall use three different words: one says the cost is high, one says it is low, and a printed report gives a figure for the cost itself. What does that set of three show?

options.text: High, low and cost are three separate ideas, and the report is the formal one
High and low are two names for one idea, and the report repeats the same one
options.misconception: collapses a judgement about cost and a figure for cost into a single idea

options.text: The two shopfront words are the formal ones, and the printed report is casual
options.misconception: gets the register exactly backwards for all three words

options.text: All three are the same word, differing only in how politely they are spoken
options.misconception: believes three distinct words are only three tones of one word

questions.explanation: The two shopfront words judge a cost, one calling it high and one calling it low, and the same word for high also means precious or esteemed, so a reader has to look at the neighbouring word to know which sense is in play. The word in the report is a neutral noun naming the cost itself, and it is the one that appears in the phrase for asking what something costs and in the phrase for a price list. A learner who treats the two judgements as one word has also missed that high and low are opposites, and a learner who reaches for the noun in a shop sign has chosen a word a shop would not normally put up.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three names a figure rather than passing a judgement on it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify which part of a written Chinese name is the family name
questions.stem: A Chinese name is written with three characters, and a learner has to explain to a class which part of it is the family name. What does the writing show about the order?

options.text: The family name comes first, and the given name follows as one or two characters
The given name comes first, and the family name is written at the very end
options.misconception: puts the family name last, the way an English name is arranged

options.text: The family name comes last, and the first character is always the given name
options.misconception: reverses the order while sounding as though it were decided

options.text: Both halves are given names, and one of them is a courtesy name used in writing
options.misconception: invents a third name function to avoid admitting a family name

questions.explanation: The family name comes first and the given name follows, and the given name is either one character or two, which is why three-character names are the commonest shape of all. The order holds in speech as well as in writing, so a speaker introducing themselves gives the family name first and then the given name, and a foreigner with a two-part name is expected to follow the same order. A small number of family names consist of two characters rather than one, and those are written as one block with no marker, which is a genuine trap for a learner who assumes the first character alone is the family name.
questions.hint: Ask which part a speaker states first when giving their own name aloud.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: allow a two-character family name inside the family-name position
questions.stem: A speaker gives a full name in two halves, saying first that the family name is 欧阳 and then that the given name is 子山. What does that arrangement show about how a name is built?

options.text: The family name comes first, and it may be made of more than one character
The given name comes first, and it is the part that is written with two characters
options.misconception: misplaces the two-character part by assuming the given name comes first

options.text: The family name comes last, and the two characters are read as a courtesy name
options.misconception: claims a courtesy name and puts the family name in the wrong slot

options.text: Neither half is a name, since only the first character is ever used in speech
options.misconception: believes a two-character family name is always shortened to one character

questions.explanation: The two-character surnames are descendants of older aristocratic titles, and a few of them, such as this one and the one written with the characters for sī and mǎ, are still in everyday use. They occupy the family-name slot in full, so the name is three characters long while still being one character of family name and two of given name, which is why an outsider who guesses from the shape of the name usually guesses wrong. Outside the home the person is often addressed by the given name alone, which adds a second layer of difficulty for anyone who has to read the name on a form.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the arrangement a three-character name would push into the second slot.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why two words are needed where English uses one
questions.stem: An English speaker has to say that a woman has a brother who is older than her, and one English word will not do the job. Why does the language need two words?

options.text: One word names an older brother and the other names a younger one, and both are required
One word covers both, and the age is settled by the tone the speaker uses
options.misconception: believes a single word leaves the older and younger case to intonation

options.text: Relational terms are used at all, where English has no word for a brother at all
options.misconception: denies that English has a term for a sibling at all

options.text: The older brother is named inside the word and the younger one is left unnamed
options.misconception: thinks only one of the two relationships is actually named in the language

questions.explanation: Age relative to the speaker is built into the words themselves, so a brother is named with one word if he is older and another if he is younger, and both are the ordinary everyday words rather than literary terms. The same split runs through sisters, and it also runs through the words for older and younger in the same generation, which is why a family description in this language is so much more precise than its English translation. A learner who uses one word for both loses a distinction that family members themselves rely on, and one who uses the older word for a younger brother has said something that is simply not true.
questions.hint: Ask what single piece of information a relative's word would have to carry if there were only one.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain the precision of the set of words for the English word uncle
questions.stem: A learner asks how many words the language has for the English word uncle, and learns that a father's older brother, a father's younger brother and a mother's brother each have their own. What does that pattern show?

options.text: Each relationship is named exactly, and English collapses the whole group into one word
The words differ only in politeness, and the relationships themselves go unnamed
options.misconception: reads lexical precision as though it were a matter of courtesy

options.text: Only the two on the father's side have separate words, and the rest share one
options.misconception: believes the mother's side is not distinguished in the vocabulary

options.text: There is one word for all of them, and tone alone separates the three cases
options.misconception: assumes one word covers three relationships with tone doing the work

questions.explanation: Chinese kinship vocabulary is organised by exactly which relative is involved, and the same relative reached from the mother's side is a different word from the one reached from the father's side, which is a distinction English makes in a single compound such as uncle-in-law. The set of words for the English uncle is at least five, covering the two brothers on the father's side, the brother on the mother's side, and the two husbands of a father's or a mother's sister. A learner who learns the words as isolated vocabulary without the map of who stands where soon mixes them up, because nothing in the sound points to the relationship.
questions.hint: Ask which piece of the family tree each of the words is actually pointing at.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why one word names both a grandmother and a much younger stepmother
questions.stem: A single word is used in one family both for a man's father's mother and for a young woman married to his father's father. Which word serves both, and why?

options.text: The word for a grandmother, which on the father's side can also mean a stepmother
The word for a mother, shared by a man's own mother and by his father's wife
options.misconception: moves the ambiguity onto the two women who are a generation apart

options.text: The word for an aunt, used for any older woman living inside one household
options.misconception: widens the word to a whole category of women in a home

options.text: The word for a wife, used for a grandmother and for a young stepmother alike
options.misconception: ignores the generation that the word actually names

questions.explanation: The word for a grandmother on the father's side does double duty, because in an earlier period a man might marry a woman young enough to be his own age, and from the children's point of view that woman occupies the grandmother's slot. The word for a grandmother on the mother's side does not have this second sense, since that relationship runs through blood, and the words for the two grandmothers are therefore different. The result is a genuine ambiguity that a speaker resolves by context, and it is a good example of kinship vocabulary recording a social history rather than only a family tree.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two women are in the same generation as each other's children.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the extra information carried by the two words for a brother's wife
questions.stem: English has one term for the wife of a brother, and the language has two that also say which brother it is. What does that extra information give the listener?

options.text: The rank of the husband, since the two distinguish an elder from a younger brother
The marital status of the woman, since one word implies that she is divorced
options.misconception: reads a word about rank as though it were about a divorce

options.text: The age of the woman, since the two split by whether she is over fifty
options.misconception: believes the split is by the woman's age rather than her husband's

options.text: The number of children, since the two words record whether she has any at all
options.misconception: invents a difference about children to explain two separate words

questions.explanation: The wife of an elder brother and the wife of a younger brother are named by two different words, and the deciding fact is the husband's own rank in the sibling line, not anything about the woman. The same logic produces a separate word for the wife of a younger brother that does not exist in the elder direction, because the younger brother's wife is the one who comes into a family that is already established. English compresses all of this into a single compound, which is why a translation of Chinese family conversation often has to choose and loses a distinction the speakers were relying on.
questions.hint: Ask which member of the sibling line the two women married into.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what the two words for cousin track that the English word does not
questions.stem: A family tree puts one cousin reached through the father in one column and another reached through the mother in another, and the two go into different words. What does the language track there?

options.text: Whether the shared ancestor is on the father's side, which the English word hides
The age of the cousin, since one word is reserved for an older cousin only
options.misconception: believes the split is by age rather than by which side connects them

options.text: Whether the cousin is married, since one word is reserved for a married cousin
options.misconception: invents a distinction about marriage that the words do not carry

options.text: How far away the cousin lives, since one word means a cousin living abroad
options.misconception: reads a difference of family line as though it were about geography

questions.explanation: A cousin on the father's side shares a family name with you, because you share a grandfather, and gets the word for that side. A cousin reached through the mother gets a different word, and so does a cousin reached through a father's sister, whose children carry a different family name even though they are on the father's side. English has one word for all of these, and it is also gender-neutral, so a translation into English has to choose what to keep and what to lose, and a translation the other way has to guess. The side of the tree is therefore the fact the vocabulary is recording, not the age or the distance.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two cousins would carry the same family name as each other.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain a change in a word's meaning between an older text and present speech
questions.stem: In older writing the word now used for going along on foot could also mean to run, and an old phrase about riding a horse at a gallop still contains it. What does that show about the word?

options.text: Its meaning has narrowed over time, so a modern gloss hides what it once meant
It has two separate meanings today, and the older one has not gone anywhere
options.misconception: believes both the old and the new senses are available in speech now

options.text: It always covered both, and the difference is only in how formal the tone is
options.misconception: turns a change of meaning into a difference of politeness

options.text: The older meaning belonged to a different word written with the same character
options.misconception: escapes the evidence by claiming the old writer meant a different word

questions.explanation: The everyday meaning of the word moved from running to walking on foot, and a phrase that still exists in modern speech, the one about riding a horse at a gallop, is now understood as a set expression rather than as a literal statement about running. This is the ordinary way words work: the general term for a broad action loses its edge and settles onto the most typical member of that action, so a word that once covered both running and walking ends up meaning only walking. The reason a learner meets the old meaning in a text is that the older sense is preserved in the writing even after the speech has moved on.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two activities the word used to cover before it settled on one of them.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: notice an adjective used as a general intensifier rather than as a judgement
questions.stem: A speaker says that something is 好大, in a sentence about a fish, and a learner expects a judgement about quality. What has happened to the word?

options.text: It has broadened into an intensifier, so it means very rather than good here
It still means good, and the speaker is complimenting the size of the fish
options.misconception: keeps the original sense and invents a compliment nobody offered

options.text: It has become a filler with no content at all before the noun in that position
options.misconception: over-corrects and treats the word as pure padding in every slot

options.text: It has narrowed to mean only that a thing is pleasing to look at
options.misconception: narrows the word to appearance and misses the intensifier use

questions.explanation: The word began as an adjective of quality and has spread into a general magnifier, so before an adjective or an adverb it very often means simply very, and in front of a noun it carries a surprising amount of emphasis: the same word can make a thing look big, take a long time or be early. This is why a sentence about a large fish is a natural place for it and why a learner who expects a judgement hears praise that was never offered. The other part of the history is the opposite movement, from an intensifier into a respectful prefix before a name or a title, which is the sense a learner meets when an older colleague is addressed in a certain way.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker is praising the fish or simply saying how big it is.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: tell apart a respectful prefix that applies to people from a fixed compound
questions.stem: A speaker calls an older colleague 老张 and an older friend 老李, but says 老虎 when a tiger is mentioned. What decides which of the three senses is in play?

options.text: The sense follows whether the rest of the word names a person, so a tiger is not one
The sense follows the pitch, so the three versions are told apart by the voice
options.misconception: believes a tone change decides between the respectful and the literal sense

options.text: The sense follows the number of characters, so any two-character word is fixed
options.misconception: decides by word length and so rules out the respectful uses

options.text: The sense follows whether the sentence is spoken aloud or written down at all
options.misconception: believes the distinction is about speech rather than about meaning

questions.explanation: The prefix started as a plain adjective for old and then spread outwards: in front of a surname or a title it is a respectful form of address, so it can be attached to a colleague, a teacher or a family friend, and in front of another word it can be a strong intensifier meaning very. Words like the one for tiger are single words in their own right, and the character for old is simply part of the word rather than a prefix doing any work, which is why the same character behaves so differently in the three cases. The test for a learner is to ask whether the second part names a person that somebody could address.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second part of each word could be something you call a person.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what the respectful form of you does to the distance between speakers
questions.stem: A shop assistant addresses a customer as 您 and then addresses a close friend as 你 in the same afternoon. What is the choice of word doing in each case?

options.text: It sets the distance between the speakers, from respectful through to familiar
It marks how many people are being addressed, one form being the plural
options.misconception: reads the respectful form as though it were a number marker

options.text: It marks the age of the person addressed, one form being reserved for the old
options.misconception: confuses politeness with age, which the two forms do not track

options.text: It marks the topic of the conversation, one form being used for business matters
options.misconception: believes the pronoun is chosen by the subject under discussion

questions.explanation: The respectful form is used for customers, for elders, for teachers and for strangers in a situation where formality is expected, and the familiar form is used between people who already know each other well. The distance is social, not grammatical, and it shifts during a conversation: a shopkeeper may open with the respectful form and switch to the familiar one once a conversation has warmed up, which a learner who treats the choice as fixed finds hard to predict. One detail is worth knowing, since there is no polite plural, the verb after the respectful form does not take the plural suffix that several other pronouns do.
questions.hint: Ask how well the two speakers know each other, and who is expected to show more respect.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: sort a pair of question words into its formal member and its colloquial member
questions.stem: A formal report writes whether a plan works and where the money went, while a colleague asks the same two things casually. Which pair does the language actually use?

options.text: A single word for each question in the report, and a two-syllable one in speech
A two-syllable word for each question in the report, and a single one in speech
options.misconception: reverses which member of each pair is the formal one

options.text: The same single word in both, since formality cannot affect a question word
options.misconception: believes a question word is immune to register differences

options.text: Two different words in each pair, so neither question keeps a single form
options.misconception: answers with four words where the language uses two per pair

questions.explanation: Both pairs work the same way. For whether, a report uses a single written question word while a conversation uses the two-part version that sounds like asking twice. For where, a report uses a single written word while speech uses the shorter colloquial form, and there is a third variant that sounds still more formal. The distinction is not about correctness, since speakers mix the forms freely, but about what the choice signals: a written report is expected to sound considered, and a colleague in a corridor is not. A learner who uses the formal word in speech sounds stiff rather than wrong.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two speakers is writing something down for other people to read.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: separate a word for troubling somebody from a word for requesting a favour
questions.stem: A speaker apologises for troubling somebody, and a colleague elsewhere asks a favour with more insistence. Which two words fit those two jobs?

options.text: The word for troubling a person, and the word for requesting a favour of them
The word for requesting a favour, and the word for troubling a person
options.misconception: swaps the two jobs while keeping both words as the right set

options.text: Two words for troubling a person, differing only in how they are written
options.misconception: claims a request and an apology are distinguished by spelling alone

options.text: The word for apologising, and the word for thanking somebody afterwards
options.misconception: replaces the request with thanks and leaves a favour unasked

questions.explanation: The word for troubling a person carries an apology in it, so putting it in front of somebody's name, or in front of a verb, is a way of saying sorry to bother you and it is the standard phrase for asking a colleague for help. The word for requesting a favour is more insistently a request and carries less apology, so it suits a bigger ask. A third word in this family means that you have gone to the trouble, and it is the one a speaker reaches for when thanking someone for effort. All three are polite, and the choice among them says how big the ask is.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two speakers is apologising and which is simply asking.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a casual borrowed farewell from the neutral one
questions.stem: Two colleagues part outside the office. One waves and says a short borrowed farewell, the other says the longer everyday farewell and mentions next time. What does the difference mark?

options.text: One is a casual borrowing used among friends, the other the neutral everyday farewell
One is the formal farewell, the other the casual borrowing used among friends
options.misconception: gets the register of the two farewells exactly backwards

options.text: Both are formal, and the longer one also promises a next meeting
options.misconception: claims a casual borrowing is the more formal of the two

options.text: Both are casual, and only the longer one can be used in writing at all
options.misconception: denies that a spoken borrowing can appear in writing

questions.explanation: The short borrowed farewell is a Chinese rendering of two English words said twice, and it belongs to casual speech among people who are comfortable with each other; it appears in a message rather than in a formal letter. The longer everyday farewell is neutral, it is what a speaker uses in almost any parting, and adding a mention of next time turns it into a warmer version. A learner who reaches for the short form with a stranger sounds overfamiliar, and one who writes it in a formal message has used a form that belongs to speech.
questions.hint: Ask how well the two speakers know each other, and which version could go in a letter.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state the effect the light child-suffix has on a spoken word
questions.stem: A speaker pronounces the word for a small child and the word for smell with a light extra syllable that a textbook does not print, and both sound warmer and more familiar. What is that suffix doing?

options.text: It softens the word and makes it familiar, and sometimes makes it smaller
It makes the word more formal, because the extra sound marks respect for the topic
options.misconception: reads a spoken softening as though it added formality or respect

options.text: It turns the word into a plural, since the extra sound marks more than one thing
options.misconception: treats the extra syllable as a number marker rather than a softener

options.text: It restores an older reading, so the suffixed form is the more literary one
options.misconception: believes the extra syllable returns a word to an archaic sense

questions.explanation: This suffix is a vowel added to the end of a syllable, and it does two things that learners often expect to be separate. It very often makes a word sound small, affectionate or casual, which is why it turns up on the word for a child and on the word for smell and on the word for a little thing. And it also just loosens the register, so a great many words carry it with no sense of smallness at all, and speakers use it by habit. It is also largely a feature of speech rather than of writing, and it is more common in the north, so a learner who meets it everywhere in a novel and nowhere in a textbook has met one register rather than the language.
questions.hint: Ask how the speaker would sound if the extra syllable were left off in each case.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: exclude the two words where the light suffix is not a diminutive at all
questions.stem: A learner assumes that every two-character word whose second syllable sounds like the light suffix is a diminutive, and then has to explain the two obvious exceptions. Which pair are they?

options.text: The words for daughter and son, where the syllable keeps its own full tone
The words for flower and smell, where the suffix really does make them smaller
options.misconception: names the clearest examples of the suffix as though they were the exceptions

options.text: The words for elder and younger, where the syllable marks age rather than size
options.misconception: confuses the diminutive suffix with the two words that compare ages

options.text: The words for today and a while back, where the suffix is a grammatical particle
options.misconception: claims the suffix is a particle in a set of ordinary time expressions

questions.explanation: The two words for daughter and son contain that sound but not that suffix, and the difference is measurable: in both the syllable keeps a full tone, and the writing of the word for daughter even shows it with a mark that tells the reader to pronounce it fully. A softener is always short and light, and a full tone is the opposite of that, so the test a learner can apply is the tone rather than the sound. Getting this right matters beyond the two words, because the same test tells a reader whether an unfamiliar two-character word is being made smaller or is simply a word that happens to end that way.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second syllable in each word is short and light or carries a tone of its own.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: classify the shared ending of a set of place and object nouns
questions.stem: A learner sees that the words for stone, bone, steamed bun and a piece of wood all end in the same short unstressed syllable. What kind of element is that shared ending?

options.text: A suffix that builds a family of concrete nouns, read in the neutral tone
A full second syllable of each word, carrying its own tone in every case
options.misconception: misses that the ending carries no tone of its own anywhere in the set

options.text: A classifier that must move to the front of the phrase before these nouns
options.misconception: confuses a word-forming suffix with the classifier that counts the noun

options.text: A single word borrowed whole and added to four separate native roots
options.misconception: invents a loan to explain a productive native pattern

questions.explanation: That ending is a suffix, and the four words are a family built with it, each one naming something with a shape or a mass. It is always short and light, which is why a learner who expects a tone mark on it never finds one, and a speaker who gives it a full tone sounds odd. The suffix is productive, so a learner who knows it can often guess the meaning of an unfamiliar word that contains it, which is a real shortcut. The trap is that a few common words merely start with the same two characters, most obviously the word for hair, where the second part is an ordinary full-tone syllable and not the suffix at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the final syllable in those four words ever takes a tone of its own.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: accept that the set of nouns taking a common suffix has to be learned rather than predicted
questions.stem: A learner collects six nouns that end in the same short unstressed syllable, notices that several similar-looking nouns do not, and asks for a rule. What is the honest answer?

options.text: The ending is a matter of which roots habitually take it, so the set must be learned
Every made object takes the ending, and no natural thing ever takes it
options.misconception: believes a made-versus-natural rule predicts the whole set

options.text: The ending is added whenever the noun is longer than one syllable in writing
options.misconception: thinks word length in characters decides which nouns take the ending

options.text: The ending marks plurals, so a noun carrying it means more than one of the thing
options.misconception: reads a noun-forming suffix as though it were a plural marker

questions.explanation: The ending began as a diminutive, added to a small or a dear thing, and over centuries it stopped meaning anything about size and simply became a general way of making a noun, so it now attaches to some roots and not to others for no reason a learner can derive. The words for table, chair, plate, bottle, hat and cup all take it, while the words for fish, cat, book and apple do not, and nothing about made objects or word length predicts which group a word falls into. It is still useful to know, because a noun you have not met often contains this ending, and knowing it tells you the word is an everyday thing rather than an abstract one.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is any feature of the two groups of nouns that could predict membership.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what repeating a two-syllable adjective does to its strength
questions.stem: A speaker says a four-syllable form of clean about a table, and a learner expects a mild word meaning simply clean. What has the repetition done to the meaning?

options.text: It has strengthened the word, so the table is spotless rather than only clean
It has weakened the word, so the table is only fairly clean after all
options.misconception: assumes repetition always softens, which is true of verbs and not adjectives

options.text: It has turned the word into a plural, naming several clean tables at once
options.misconception: reads an intensified adjective as though it were a number marker

options.text: It has marked the sentence as a question about whether the table is clean
options.misconception: believes a reduplicated adjective signals doubt about a claim

questions.explanation: Repeating a two-syllable adjective strengthens it to mean entirely so, so the four-syllable form about the table says the table is spotless, with no trace of dirt anywhere. The same pattern gives a cheerful form for happy and a smooth form for smooth, and a native speaker uses them freely. The four-syllable version is the one that appears in writing, while the shortened two-syllable version is what most people actually say, and the two mean the same thing. A learner who treats repetition as a softener everywhere will get this exactly backwards, because softening is what it does to verbs.
questions.hint: Ask whether repetition in this position makes the quality more complete or less complete.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: separate the softening effect of a repeated verb from a second action
questions.stem: A speaker says the repeated form of look and the repeated form of think where a textbook would print the plain verbs, and a learner wonders whether two separate actions are meant. What does the repetition contribute?

options.text: It makes the action brief and casual, softening the request rather than adding meaning
It adds a second action, so the speaker is really asking for two things to be done
options.misconception: takes a repeated verb as two separate events rather than one softened one

options.text: It marks the action as finished, so the looking is now completely in the past
options.misconception: reads the second syllable as a completion marker rather than part of the verb

options.text: It makes the action polite and formal, as though a stranger were being asked
options.misconception: believes a casual softening makes a request more formal and not less

questions.explanation: A repeated verb makes the action sound shorter, lighter and more casual, so the repeated form of look means have a look rather than look carefully at it, and the repeated form of try is gentler than the plain verb. The second syllable is normally short and unstressed, which is part of the softening. It is not a second action, and it is not a completion marker either. The pattern is so productive that almost any verb can be repeated this way, and adding the word for a while beforehand softens it further, so the effect is available at three strengths rather than one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker wants a long careful action or a short casual one.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: recognise that a repeated noun means every one of its members
questions.stem: A speaker uses a repeated word for person and a repeated word for day in a sentence about a community, and a learner takes both for ordinary plurals. What are the two forms actually doing?

options.text: Each one means every single member, spreading the word across the whole group
Each one is a polite plural, and the plain word would sound far too familiar
options.misconception: reads a distributive meaning as though it were a matter of politeness

options.text: Each one marks a rough number, so the speaker cannot be exact about how many
options.misconception: believes repetition signals vagueness rather than universality

options.text: Each one is a formal written form that spoken language always shortens
options.misconception: claims the spoken form is the shortened one and both are written

questions.explanation: Repeating a one-syllable noun gives it a distributive sense, so the repeated form of person means every person without exception and the repeated form of day means every day, and the same works for year and for place. A plural would leave room for exceptions, and a rough number would be vague, and this form does neither: it is emphatic and complete. There is a neighbouring pattern worth knowing, where the word for one is put in front twice instead, and that one means one at a time, so a learner who mixes the two patterns will say that things were done one at a time when the meaning was every one of them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the form allows exceptions and whether it gives a number at all.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why a familiar one-character abbreviation has no equivalent at the top of the school
questions.stem: A school notice shortens the names of the three stages of schooling to single characters, and a learner asks why the same shortening is not available for the stage above them. Why is that?

options.text: The three shorten longer official names, and the highest stage has no such short form
The three are nicknames, so the highest stage must always be written out in full
options.misconception: confuses a standard short form of an official name with a private nickname

options.text: All four shorten official names, but the highest stage one is too rare to shorten
options.misconception: denies a short form that exists and is used for the highest stage

options.text: The three are written that way only on timetables and never in running text
options.misconception: restricts a common short form to one kind of document

questions.explanation: The three short forms are the first character of a longer official name, and the first character of each of those official names is already a complete word: the word for small, and the first character of the words for junior and for senior secondary. The stage above them, the university, is not written with a first character that can stand alone, so the single character for big is not a short form of it and a notice saying so would be heard as a joke. Related short forms follow the same pattern, such as the two characters for attached and the two for vocational, each of them standing for a longer official title.
questions.hint: Ask whether the first character of each official name is itself a whole word.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: expand two well-known short forms of university names
questions.stem: A speaker says 北大 and 清华 in a list of two universities, and a learner who has never visited asks what each short form stands for. What are the two of them?

options.text: Two universities in the capital, each shortened by keeping its distinctive characters
Two districts of the capital, named after the schools located inside them
options.misconception: misreads a short form of a school name as the name of a district

options.text: Two nicknames for one university, used by different generations of speakers
options.misconception: assumes two well-known short forms name the same institution

options.text: A shorthand for a school and a ministry, in that order as they were said
options.misconception: reads one short form as a government department rather than a university

questions.explanation: Both are universities in the capital, and both short forms work by keeping the one or two characters that distinguish the school from its neighbours, dropping the words for country and university that the full names share. The second one is not simply the first two characters of its full name, which shows that the short form was fixed by usage rather than by a rule, and that is worth knowing before a learner tries to build one. Several such short forms are ambiguous, and a learner who meets two of them for different institutions in one document has to use the surrounding words rather than the short form itself to tell them apart.
questions.hint: Ask which characters the two full names have that the short forms have thrown away.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: resolve an ambiguous short form from the surrounding context
questions.stem: A speaker says the same two-character short form twice in one morning, once about a university and once about a national body, and a learner is sure it is one thing. What settles it?

options.text: The surrounding words, because the short form can name either a university or a body
The pitch, because the two uses are marked by a different tone on the last syllable
options.misconception: expects a tone difference between two uses of the same two characters

options.text: The number of strokes, because one version is written with a different character
options.misconception: invents two different written forms for what is one short form

options.text: The age of the speaker, because only younger people use it for the university
options.misconception: believes usage is split by generation rather than by context

questions.explanation: The short form is genuinely ambiguous, because it can stand for the people's university or for the people's congress, and the two belong to completely different worlds: one is an institution of higher education and the other is the body that writes the country's laws. Nothing in the two characters themselves distinguishes them, so the surrounding words have to do the work, and a learner who meets the short form without them will guess. This is a good example of a general principle about short forms in the language: the shorter a name gets, the more context it needs to be understood.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker is talking about in each of the two sentences.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a regional vocabulary difference between two speakers of the same language
questions.stem: A speaker in the north of the country calls a root vegetable 土豆, while a speaker in the south calls the same vegetable by a longer name. What kind of difference is this?

options.text: A regional difference in vocabulary, and both words are in normal use nationally
A difference in register, where one word is formal and the other is slang
options.misconception: reads a regional difference as though it were a difference in politeness

options.text: A difference in meaning, since the two words name two different vegetables
options.misconception: takes two names for one plant as though they were two plants

options.text: A difference in script alone, since both words are written with the same characters
options.misconception: describes the writing as the same when the two words are written differently

questions.explanation: The two names are for one vegetable, and the difference is where people say them: the short name is what most northerners and most younger speakers nationwide use now, while the longer name, which is also what the neighbouring languages call it, is what many southerners still say and what formal writing still prefers. Neither speaker is being odd, and neither word is slang. The same pattern runs through other everyday foods, and it is a good warning for a learner: recognising that a word is regional rather than wrong is often the whole difficulty in understanding a speaker from another part of the country.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words a speaker from the other region would also understand.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: recognise a loan of an English phrase as the regional form for a hired car
questions.stem: A visitor hears two words for the same hired car in two cities, one of them a rendering of an English phrase heard through Cantonese. Which pair is the loan, and where does it belong?

options.text: The loan belongs to the south around Canton, and the other word is used elsewhere
The loan belongs to the north, and the other word is used in the south instead
options.misconception: puts the southern loan in the north and the standard word in the south

options.text: The loan is a written form only, and the other word is the spoken one everywhere
options.misconception: treats a spoken southern loan as though it were only ever written

options.text: The two words name two things, a taxi and a hired car that includes the driver
options.misconception: invents a difference in what is hired rather than a difference of region

questions.explanation: The two characters for hired car in the south come from an English word for taxicab, heard through Cantonese and then written with Chinese characters, and they are perfectly normal there and in the neighbouring special administrative regions. The three-character word elsewhere is the standard national term and is what a traveller will meet in most of the country. The same borrowing pattern shows up with buses, where a two-character word from the English word for bus is again a southern usage. A learner who meets either word while travelling should recognise it as regional rather than as an error or a private coinage.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the country the English phrase reached first and through which port.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: accept that one word splits its meaning differently in two regions
questions.stem: A southern speaker uses a two-character word for plain cooked rice and its single-character form for a meal, while a northern speaker uses that single character for plain rice. What does that split show?

options.text: A regional difference inside one word, so a translation must decide which sense is meant
A difference in politeness, with the northern sense being the more casual of the two
options.misconception: turns a regional difference in meaning into a difference in tone

options.text: A difference in meaning, since the two speakers are eating genuinely different rice
options.misconception: mistakes two readings of one word for two kinds of food

options.text: A difference in script, since the two words are written with different characters
options.misconception: claims two written forms where the difference is one word read two ways

questions.explanation: In the south the single character means a meal, so plain rice needs the two-character form, and a sentence about eating uses it to mean the meal; in the north the single character means plain rice, so a sentence about eating it uses the same character for what the southern speaker would call a meal. The two are perfectly clear within their own region, which is the point: neither speaker has to think about it. For a learner this is the sharpest kind of regional difference to meet, because a single word has two jobs in two places rather than two words for one thing, and a translation that ignores the region loses the meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what a speaker in each region thinks is being counted when the word is used.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a festival from its three best-known customs
questions.stem: A family describes what they did on the first evening of the year, and the list includes a set meal, red packets containing money, and staying up late. Which festival is this, and what are those three things?

options.text: The spring festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, money gifts, and staying up
The lantern festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, money gifts, and staying up
options.misconception: gives the spring festival's customs to the lantern festival

options.text: The mid-autumn festival, whose customs are round pastries, lanterns, and a night outing
options.misconception: describes a different festival entirely rather than misplacing the customs

options.text: The dragon boat festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, boat races, and dumplings
options.misconception: mixes the reunion dinner of one festival with the races of another

questions.explanation: The spring festival is the one that opens the lunar year, and the three customs in the list belong to it: the reunion dinner on the evening before the first day, the red packets of money given to children and to elderly relatives, and staying up into the night to see the new year in. Two of the names are also worth keeping straight, since the festival itself and the custom of staying up are two different words. The lantern festival comes two weeks later and belongs to the fifteenth day, and the mid-autumn and dragon boat festivals belong to later months again, so the first evening of the year belongs to none of them.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four festivals opens the year according to the lunar calendar.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify a festival and its food from the moon in the name
questions.stem: A festival is named after the moon, and its customs include a round baked food eaten at night while people sit outside looking up at the sky. Which festival is it, and what is the food?

options.text: The mid-autumn festival, and the food is the round pastry eaten on that night
The spring festival, and the food is the round pastry eaten on that night
options.misconception: gives the moon festival's food to the festival that opens the year

options.text: The lantern festival, and the food is the sweet soup eaten on that night
options.misconception: confuses a sweet soup with the baked pastry and the festival with it

options.text: The dragon boat festival, and the food is the leaf-wrapped rice eaten on that day
options.misconception: gives the boat festival's food to the festival named after the moon

questions.explanation: The mid-autumn festival is named for the middle of the eighth month and for the moon, and its food is the round baked pastry that is cut into pieces and shared, so that the sharing and the roundness both carry meaning. Looking up at the moon on that night is the other great custom, and the story of a woman who flies to the moon is told along with it. None of the other three festivals is named for the moon, and their foods are quite different: a sweet filled ball of glutinous rice, a leaf-wrapped parcel of rice, and the reunion dinner of the new year.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four festivals takes its name from a body in the sky.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: connect a festival to the poet whose death it is said to remember
questions.stem: A festival is tied to a poet of the warring states period who drowned himself in a river, and its customs include a leaf-wrapped parcel of rice and boat races. Which festival is it?

options.text: The dragon boat festival, said to remember a named poet who drowned in a river
The mid-autumn festival, said to remember a named poet who drowned in a river
options.misconception: gives the river and the poet to the festival that is named for the moon

options.text: The spring festival, said to remember a named poet who drowned in a river
options.misconception: attaches the poet and the river to the festival that opens the year

options.text: The lantern festival, said to remember a named poet who drowned in a river
options.misconception: attaches the poet and the river to the festival of lanterns

questions.explanation: The dragon boat festival is traditionally linked to the poet whose name is 屈原, a minister of the state of Chu in the warring states period who drowned himself in a river after his state was defeated, and the legend says the local people raced boats to try to save him and threw rice into the water so that the fish would not eat him. Both customs therefore point at the same story. He is also the poet associated with the earliest great collection of songs from Chu, so the festival, the food and the literature all hang together. That makes this the one festival in the year that commemorates a named individual rather than a season or a date.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four festivals is about a person rather than about a season.

questions.learningObjective: identify a festival from its date and its three customs
questions.stem: A festival falls on the fifteenth day of the first month of the lunar year, and its customs include lanterns, riddles written on those lanterns, and a sweet filled ball of rice. Which festival is this?

options.text: The lantern festival, marked by lanterns, lantern riddles, and a sweet filled ball
The mid-autumn festival, marked by lanterns, riddles, and a sweet filled ball
options.misconception: gives the fifteenth day of the first month to the eighth month festival

options.text: The spring festival, marked by lanterns, riddles, and a sweet filled ball
options.misconception: attaches the lantern customs to the festival that opens the year

options.text: The double ninth festival, marked by lanterns, riddles, and a sweet filled ball
options.misconception: confuses a ninth-day festival with the fifteenth day of the first month

questions.explanation: The fifteenth day of the first month is the lantern festival, which closes the long run of new year celebrations that began with the spring festival a fortnight earlier. Lanterns, riddles written on the lanterns or hung outside a gate, and a sweet filled ball of glutinous rice are its three best-known customs, and the same two characters name the festival and the food, which is a nice example of one word doing both jobs. Lantern festivals are also held on other dates in different places, and the ninth day of the ninth month has its own festival, so a learner should check the month before trusting the word.

questions.learningObjective: order the stages of a formal banquet by the sequence the dishes arrive
questions.stem: A formal banquet is described in four stages, and the host is asking which order the dishes actually arrive in. Which of the four orders is the traditional one?

options.text: Cold dishes, then hot dishes, then soup, and the staple food at the very end
The staple food, then cold dishes, then hot dishes, and soup at the end
options.misconception: puts the staple first, which is the order of a modern self-service meal

options.text: Cold dishes, then soup, then hot dishes, and the staple food at the end
options.misconception: serves the soup too early, before the hot dishes have been eaten

options.text: Hot dishes, then cold dishes, then the staple food, and soup at the end
options.misconception: reverses the opening pair of the traditional order

questions.explanation: A traditional banquet opens with cold dishes to pick at while people settle down, then brings the hot dishes, then the soup, and only then the staple food, with a sweet course at the very end. The staple last is the detail a learner from another cuisine finds surprising, because in a family meal rice usually appears from the start and stays on the table throughout. The count word for a dish is the same one used for a course of a meal, and the whole arrangement exists to build towards an ending, which is why a banquet is planned backwards from its last dish.
questions.hint: Ask when the rice arrives at a formal banquet, and compare that with an ordinary family meal.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a given name of a particular generation is doing
questions.stem: A name from the 1950s ends in two characters that a learner glosses as fine and outstanding, and asks what those characters are for. What is the best answer?

options.text: They record a generation's naming fashion, evoking elegance and brightness
They name a rank and a post, so the holder had an official position
options.misconception: reads a name's pleasant meanings as though they recorded a job

options.text: They name a place and a date, so they record where and when she was born
options.misconception: treats the two characters as a place name and a calendar year

options.text: They form a courtesy name, so they are used only in formal writing on a tombstone
options.misconception: assumes a given name is a formal literary name rather than a birth name

questions.explanation: The two characters in this name are chosen for their pleasant sounds and their flattering meanings, and the combination is one that an entire generation of women received, so a speaker hearing it can guess roughly how old the holder is. The character for fine or elegant and the character for outstanding both carry praise, and the generation in question named its daughters in a set of characters that are all of this kind. Nothing is recorded in a name of this sort, which is what distinguishes it from a western name, and it is why a modern speaker finds an old name's characters more informative than a modern one.
questions.hint: Ask how many people of that generation in one family were given the same two characters.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: conclude that given names record a period's fashions rather than a fixed rule
questions.stem: Two names are compared: one ends in characters that mean building the nation, and another puts an ordinary word meaning little at the front. What does that comparison between the two reveal?

options.text: That a given name records the fashions of a generation rather than a fixed naming rule
That the first name belongs to a rural family and the second to a city household
options.misconception: reads a difference of generation as a difference of where people live

options.text: That the character for little marks a poor family in the older name only
options.misconception: takes an affectionate prefix in a name as a claim about money

options.text: That the two names come from two different and unrelated languages entirely
options.misconception: supposes one name is foreign without any evidence for it

questions.explanation: The first name belongs to a generation born when building the country was the thing everybody talked about, and a large share of that generation received some version of it, so the name dates its holder as precisely as a year would. The second name belongs to a later generation, where a common word meaning little went in front of a character meaning bright as a way of sounding affectionate, and that too was shared by millions of children at once. The newest names move again, using characters lifted from classical poetry or a phrase lifted from ordinary speech. So the lesson is that there is no rule, only decades, and each of them has its own taste.
questions.hint: Ask how many people born in the same decade were given a name like each of the two.
